title: The VLT’s night light
caption: A laser guide star beneath the Large Magellanic Cloud, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Yepun, one of the four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, fires a laser beam into the dark sky over Paranal Observatory in this photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek. Above it hangs the Large Magellanic Cloud, a barred spiral galaxy in orbit around our own. A faint white glow marks its older stars, while iridescent magenta and blue show its young stellar nurseries.

The laser creates an artificial star, a Laser Guide Star, which helps astronomers cope with Earth's atmosphere. The air blurs and distorts starlight, so astronomers place the laser star near the patch of sky they are observing and measure the tiny flickers in its image.

The VLT's adaptive optics system uses that reference to correct for the shifting atmosphere, producing the sharpest possible images in the main observations. The Large Magellanic Cloud, like the Small Magellanic Cloud, has been studied many times by ESO telescopes.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken at Paranal; the source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, bringing out colours in the Large Magellanic Cloud that look grey or faint in person.

explore: Because the Magellanic Clouds are so close, their nebulae and star clusters can be seen in detail, making them rewarding targets for amateur and professional astronomers alike.
alt: A VLT telescope shooting a laser beam into the night sky, with the Large Magellanic Cloud glowing white, magenta and blue above it.
